papers.title_in_file: Efficient Frequency Doubling with Active Stabilization on Chip
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper on a thin-film lithium niobate periodically poled microring with an on-chip phase modulator, used for second-harmonic generation at about 50% absolute efficiency with Pound-Drever-Hall locking.

assertions.value: The authors report over 51 % absolute second-harmonic generation efficiency in a thin-film lithium niobate microring with 1.8 mW pump power, which they present as a new high among nanophotonic platforms at such milliwatt driving power.
quotes: we achieve over 51 % absolute SHG efficiency with only 1.8 mW pump power
scoring a new high among all nanophotonic platforms at such milliwatt level driving power
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison with other platforms rests on the authors' own survey in Figure 3(d), which they limit to milliwatt and sub-milliwatt pump results.

assertions.value: The authors report that the absolute SHG efficiency saturates at 51% with 1.8 mW on-chip pump power after correcting for the fiber-chip coupling loss.
quotes: saturates at 51% with 1.8 mW on-chip pump power after correcting for the coupling loss
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device; it depends on the coupling-loss correction.
assertions.reader_inference: The text calls this quantity the absolute SHG efficiency but writes the symbol for the normalized efficiency (a typographical slip in the paper).

assertions.value: The authors report stable SHG with conversion efficiency around 48% for over 30 minutes, using Pound-Drever-Hall locking with the on-chip phase modulator.
quotes: we demonstrate stable SHG with conversion efficiency around 48% for over 30 minutes by Pound–Drever–Hall (PDH) locking
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device and one run.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 3.3 gives a range of 48% to 41% over the run, so 'around 48%' is the starting value and not a constant.

assertions.value: The authors report that with locking engaged the absolute conversion is stabilized between 48% and 41% over 30 minutes. They attribute the slight drop mainly to coupling instability, as the pump transmission drifts downward while the feedback signal keeps feeding into the laser.
quotes: the absolute conversion is stabilized between 48% and 41% over 30 minutes
The slight drop over time is mainly due to the coupling instability
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one run; the cause is the authors' attribution.

assertions.value: The authors state in the caption of the locking-run figure that the initial absolute conversion efficiency is 48% with 1.1 mW on-chip pump power, and that locking is engaged after manually tuning the pump close to the cavity resonance.
quotes: The initial absolute conversion efficiency is 48% with 1.1 mW on-chip pump power.
The locking is engaged after manually tuning the pump close to the cavity resonance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The caption states the setup and starting condition of the locking run.
assertions.reader_inference: The 48% lock was reached at a lower on-chip pump than the 1.8 mW of the 51% saturation point.

assertions.value: The paper gives, citing earlier work, that with quasi-phase matching and no cavity detuning the highest absolute conversion efficiency is the product of the pump loaded-to-coupling quality-factor ratio and the second-harmonic loaded-to-coupling quality-factor ratio. It therefore requires over-coupling at both wavelengths.
quotes: Assuming quasi-phase matching and no cavity detuning, the highest absolute conversion efficiency is
given by [2, 18]:
Eq.(1) requires
assertions.certainty_reason: A relation the paper attributes to other work; the equation itself is garbled in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The product-of-ratios form is read from the symbols Qp,L/Qp,c and Qsh,L/Qsh,c in the garbled Eq. (1); the quotes hold only the prose around it.

assertions.value: The authors state that a high normalized efficiency (for example about 150% per mW) is important to reach a high absolute efficiency (for example about 50%) with only milliwatt pump power.
quotes: Thus, high normalized efficiency ηnor (e.g., ∼150% mW−1) is important to achieve high absolute efficiency ηabs (e.g., ∼50%) with only milliwatt pump power.
assertions.certainty_reason: A design rationale following the cited Eq. (2), whose statement is not legible in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that although thin-film lithium niobate microrings reach normalized SHG efficiency exceeding 100% per mW, the absolute conversion efficiency has been capped at 20% due to thermal, photorefractive and Zeno blockade effects. They cite earlier work for this.
quotes: exceeding 100% mW−1 [1, 2, 3, 11]
is capped at 20% due to thermal, PR, and Zeno blockade effects
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about prior work that the paper attributes to cited sources.

assertions.value: The device is fabricated on a Z-cut lithium niobate on insulator wafer with a 700-nm thick lithium niobate film bonded on a 2 µm silicon dioxide layer above a silicon substrate. The microring top width is 1.75 µm and its radius is 80 µm.
quotes: with a 700-nm thick LN thin film bonded on 2 µm silicon dioxide layer above a silicon substrate
The top width and the radius of the microring are 1.75 µm and 80 µm, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own device setup in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors report a shallow etch with 410-nm thick lithium niobate etched and 290-nm remaining, with a sidewall angle of approximately 67 degrees. The pulley coupler has a top width of 400 nm, a gap of 650 nm and a length of 80 µm. Periodic poling has a period of 4.0 µm and uses several 1-ms and 525-V electrical pulses.
quotes: 410-nm thick LN is etched with 290-nm LN remaining, and the sidewall angle is approximately 67◦
with wpulley = 400 nm, gpulley = 650 nm, and Lpulley = 80 µm
a concentric periodically poled region with a period of 4.0 µm
several 1-ms and 525-V electrical pulses
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own fabrication parameters in Section 2.

assertions.value: The phase modulator uses a ground-signal-ground electrode of 30-nm Cr and 300 nm Au. Its waveguide top width is 1.5 µm, the signal pad is 5 µm wide and the ground pads 50 µm wide with a 3 µm gap, and the effective modulation length of the electrode is 0.14 cm. The authors note that a signal pad wider than 10 µm helps reach 50 Ω impedance but reduces the overlap between the electrical field and the optical mode.
quotes: deposit 30-nm Cr and 300nm Au as the electrode material
The top width of the waveguide of the phase modulator is 1.5 µm.
The width of the signal pad and ground pad are 5 µm and 50 µm, respectively, with 3 µm gap between them.
The effective modulation length of the electrode is 0.14 cm.
a wider signal pad width (> 10 µm) helps achieving 50 Ω impedance but reduces effective overlap
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own device design in Section 2.
assertions.reader_inference: The pad-width trade-off is the authors' design statement; the paper gives no measurement of impedance versus pad width.

assertions.value: The authors report loaded, coupling and intrinsic quality factors of about 1.5, 2.1 and 5.0 (all times ten to the fifth) for the infrared mode, and loaded and intrinsic quality factors of about 0.6 and 5.6 (times ten to the fifth), with a coupling quality factor of 0.67, for the visible mode.
quotes: QL(Qc, Q0) ≈ 1.5(2.1, 5.0) × 105 for the IR mode and QL(Q0) ≈ 0.6(0.67, 5.6) × 105 for the visible mode
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the exponent flat ('105'); the value reads it as ten to the fifth. The visible coupling Q of 0.67 sits in the coupling position of the paper's own notation, and its unit is read the same way.

assertions.value: The authors state that over-coupling at both wavelengths is essential for high absolute conversion efficiency, and that the highest possible conversion efficiency for the current device is 64%. They state that near unity efficiency needs the cavity further over-coupled for both the visible and infrared modes.
quotes: For the current device, the highest possible conversion efficiency is ηabs,max = 64%.
For near unity efficiency, the cavity needs to be further overcoupled for both the visible and IR modes.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value derived from the measured quality factors through the cited Eq. (1).
assertions.reader_inference: The 64% bound is the ideal case (no detuning, quasi-phase matching); the paper says the attained value is limited by thermal and photorefractive effects.

assertions.value: The authors state that although the conversion efficiency can theoretically reach 64% for the current device, in practice the attainable absolute efficiency is limited by thermal and photorefractive effects. At on-chip pump powers over a few hundred microwatts, the light-induced static space-charge field modifies both the cavity resonance and the quasi-phase matching condition.
quotes: Although the conversion efficiency for the current device can theoretically reach 64%, in practice the attainable ηabs is limited by the thermal and photorefractive effects [22].
(e.g., over few hundreds of microwatts in this device)
assertions.certainty_reason: A mechanism the authors assert with citations; it is not isolated by an experiment here.

assertions.value: The authors report quasi-phase matched SHG for resonance modes at 1561.4 nm and 780.7 nm around 75.4 degrees Celsius, and a temperature error tolerance of 1.1 degrees Celsius for the SHG efficiency.
quotes: a quasi-phase matched SHG is achieved for optimal resonance modes at 1561.4 nm and its second-harmonic at 780.7 nm around 75.4 ◦C
shows an error tolerance of 1.1◦C
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device.

assertions.value: In the undepleted region, with 79.4 µW pump power in the input fiber and 27.5 nW second-harmonic power collected in the output fiber, the authors estimate a normalized SHG efficiency of 137, 000%/W after accounting for coupling loss and with negligible propagation loss assumed.
quotes: In the undepleted region, with 79.4 µW pump power in the input fiber, 27.5 nW SH power is collected in the output fiber.
considering negligible propagation loss, the normalized SHG efficiency ηnor is estimated to be 137, 000%/W
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: 137,000%/W equals about 137% per mW; the paper's introduction reports normalized efficiencies above 100% per mW as a class property.

assertions.value: In the depleted region, the authors report 12.6 mW pump power in the input fiber and 144 µW second-harmonic power collected in the output fiber.
quotes: In the depleted region, with 12.6 mW pump power in the input fiber, 144 µW SH power is collected in
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: These are fiber-side powers, before correction for the fiber-chip coupling losses reported in the same section.

assertions.value: The authors report fiber-chip-fiber coupling losses of 17 dB around 1560 nm and 16 dB around 780 nm.
quotes: whose losses are measured to be 17 dB around 1560 nm and 16 dB around 780 nm, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device.

assertions.value: The authors state that their comparison of absolute SHG efficiency across integrated platforms includes only milliwatt or sub-milliwatt pump results. They note that 60% at 60 mW in a silicon nitride microring and 42% at 35 mW in an aluminum nitride microring are not included because the absolute conversion there would be rather low at milliwatt pump power.
quotes: In (d) we have only included results with milliwatt or sub-millwatt pump power
There are demonstrations of 60% at 60 mW pump power in a Si3N4 microring [25] and 42% at 35 mW pump power in a AlN microring [26].
assertions.certainty_reason: The Figure 3 caption states the inclusion rule of the comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: The 'highest at milliwatt pumping' claim holds under this inclusion rule only; higher-pump results of higher efficiency exist.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that their stable frequency doubling at about 50% conversion with only milliwatt pump marks the highest by far among all nanophotonic platforms with milliwatt pumping.
quotes: it realizes stable frequency doubling at about 50% conversion with only milliwatt pump, marking the highest by far among all nanophotonic platforms with milliwatt pumping
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's comparative claim, scoped by the Figure 3(d) inclusion rule.

assertions.value: The authors state that resonance drifting occurs on a time scale from 100 µs to 10 ms, and that it may not be mitigated by self-locking, depending on the competition between thermal and photorefractive effects. They conclude this calls for active fast feedback control with bandwidth over 100 kHz.
quotes: the resonance drifting (occurring at a time scale from 100 µs to 10 ms)
This calls for an active fast feedback control with bandwidth over 100 kHz
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's design requirement, partly supported by cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that PDH stabilization needs high-speed phase modulation whose bandwidth must be comparable to or larger than the cavity linewidth (about gigahertz level), and that thin-film lithium niobate allows the phase modulator and the conversion microring to be integrated on the same chip.
quotes: whose bandwidth must be comparable or larger than cavity linewidth (about GHz level)
It allows to integrate the essential optical components
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement of a requirement and a platform advantage.

assertions.value: The authors report that a ground-signal-ground electrode scheme enhances modulation by 1.3 times over the standard ground-signal scheme, and that from an electrical field simulation in COMSOL Multiphysics the voltage-length product is estimated to be about 10 V cm, which they compare with a commercial product above 20 V cm.
quotes: to enhance our modulation by 1.3 times
the voltage-length product (Vπ ·cm) is estimated to be about 10 V·cm
Thorlab Vπ · cm > 20 V · cm
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulated estimate, not a measurement of the modulator.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no measured half-wave voltage; the 10 V cm figure comes from simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report S21 and S11 measurements with a 3-GHz vector network analyzer indicating good impedance matching of the electrodes through 3 GHz, limited by the analyzer bandwidth. The cavity linewidth is 1.25 GHz for a loaded Q of about 1.5 times ten to the fifth.
quotes: it indicates good impedance matching of the electrodes through 3 GHz, as limited by our VNA bandwidth
cavity linewidth (1.25 GHz for QL ≈ 1.5 × 105)
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device; the measurement stops at the analyzer bandwidth.
assertions.reader_inference: The modulator response above 3 GHz is not measured in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors report a clear PDH error signal observed when the telecom laser is swept across the resonance near 1561.3 nm, using 1 GHz sinusoidal modulation applied through the on-chip phase modulator and a triangle sweep of 1.5 V amplitude from the lockbox. They conclude the on-chip phase modulator functions properly.
quotes: clear PDH error signal is observed when the telecom laser is swept across the resonance around 1561.3 nm
Firstly, 1 GHz sinusoidal modulation signal is created in the RF signal generator
The ±1.5V triangle shape modulation signal is generated via the lockbox.
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says 's clear PDH error signal' and refers to Fig. 4 (d), a typographical slip; the figure shows panel (c).

assertions.value: At a scanning speed of 6 nm/s the authors observe the photorefractive effect when the on-chip laser power is above -4.5 dBm. From the response under bidirectional scanning they confirm that the photorefractive effect dominates the thermal effect with on-chip power up to +3.5 dBm.
quotes: At the scanning speed 6 nm/s, we observe the PR effect when on-chip laser power is above -4.5 dBm
we confirm that the PR effect dominates the thermal effect [7] with on-chip power up to +3.5 dBm
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device at one scan speed.

assertions.value: The authors report that their photorefractive threshold is over 10 times higher than a previously reported result in an X-cut lithium niobate microring at a similar scanning speed. They offer three possible explanations (a different wafer orientation, a higher chip temperature of 75 degrees Celsius, or the over-coupling condition) and say a future study is needed.
quotes: the threshold of the PR effect is over 10 times higher than previous reported results in X-cut LN microring at a similar scanning speed [29]
a higher chip temperature (75 ◦C), or the over-coupling condition for cavity modes, but a future study is needed
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison with one cited result; the cause is stated as unresolved.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper names three untested candidate causes, so the higher threshold is not attributed to any one of them.

assertions.value: The authors state that the photorefractive dynamic range is on the order of a millisecond and that the induced frequency shift (about gigahertz) is within the laser piezo fine-tuning range of plus or minus 8 GHz, even at very high pump power. With faster scanning (GHz per µs) through the amplitude modulation port of the Santec laser, the shift is suppressed well within the laser tuning range of plus or minus 1 GHz.
quotes: the dynamic range of the PR effect is on the order of millisecond
is within the laser piezo fine-tuning range (±8 GHz)
the PR-induced frequency shift is suppressed well within laser’s tuning range (±1 GHz)
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result from one device and one laser.

assertions.value: The authors state that PDH locking acts through the amplitude modulation port of the laser, whose speed can reach 400 KHz, and that the pump power is held within plus or minus 0.2 dB over the locking process by flattening the modulated laser power with an erbium doped fiber amplifier at fixed output.
quotes: we use the amplitude modulation port of the laser whose speed can reach 400 KHz
To stabilize the pump power within ±0.2 dB over the locking process
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.3 states the feedback setup of the locking experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The locking uses an external laser as actuator; the on-chip modulator supplies only the error signal.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lock does not hold the on-chip pump power against coupling drift, and propose as future work another feedback loop to the EDFA to stabilize it, and an additional phase modulation component on top of the microring to tune frequency in place of the external laser.
quotes: In the future, another feedback loop to the EDFA could be implemented to stabilize the on-chip pump power against the drifting of the coupling.
an additional phase modulation component could be added on top of the microring to achieve frequency tuning [30]
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.3 states the limit of the current locking scheme and the planned remedies.
assertions.reader_inference: Frequency tuning in the demonstrated lock still relies on the external laser, not on the chip.

assertions.value: The authors state that before the locking is engaged, they manually approach the resonance from red to blue and start the engagement when close to the resonance.
quotes: Before the locking is engaged, we manually approach the resonance from red to blue
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.3 states how the lock is started; acquisition is manual.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper presents no automatic lock acquisition.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they demonstrated highly efficient and actively stabilized frequency doubling by integrating a Z-cut phase modulator and a periodically poled lithium niobate microring on the same chip, with simultaneous over-coupling for both fundamental and second-harmonic modes. They expect such devices to serve quantum frequency conversion, frequency comb generation and quantum photon sources.
quotes: we have demonstrated highly efficient and actively stablized frequency doubling
with simultaneous overcoupling for both fundamental and second harmonic modes
such monolithically integrated devices will serve for practical quantum frequency conversion, frequency comb generation and quantum photon sources
assertions.certainty_reason: The conclusion of an empirical study, with a forward-looking claim.
